newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam prepares for major cabinet reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam prepares for major cabinet reshuffle.

text.p: Vietnam said on Saturday there would be soon be a ministerial reshuffle, a move likely to shed light on the country's secretive political stage for the first time since a Communist Party congress four months ago.

National Assembly Chairman and senior Politburo member Nong Duc Manh said the cabinet reshuffle, which would see older ministers stand aside for younger blood, would be more sweeping than in previous years.
"In the coming days the government will present a ministerial reshuffle," Manh told reporters during a break in a National Assembly session. "This time it concerns, in particular, older people."
The government normally reshuffles the cabinet at the end of the National Assembly's month-long Autumn session which takes place from around mid-October to mid-November.

Last year it overhauled the government structure by merging eight departments to form three new super-ministries, a move aimed at cutting red tape, and named several newcomers to the line-up of ministers.
Manh said there would be no government restructuring this time and the reshuffle would not affect the prime minister or the three deputy prime ministers.
"This time...there will only be changes of ministers, not of high-ranking leaders," said Manh.
Changes to the cabinet, which have to be approved by the lawmaking National Assembly, are widely expected at ministries with economic portfolios as well as the powerful Interior (Police) Ministry.

The choice of ministers could help illustrate the political climate that emerged from the party congress, which analysts say was preceded by intense debate over the pace and scope of further reform and jockeying for seats in the Politburo.
Contrary to many predictions, the ruling triumvirate of party secretary general, president and prime minister -- all men in their seventies -- remained in place after the congress.

However, there was a shake-up and slight expansion of the Politburo, which bolstered the presence of people from security and defence-related backgrounds. Three of those people were also appointed to an elite Standing Board of five men.
Manh, who is ranked fourth in the Politburo, said National Assembly delegates had tackled the problem of corruption in the first two weeks of the current session.
Two members of the traditionally compliant assembly earlier this week called for cabinet members to explain allegations of corruption in their ministries.

State-controlled media has also taken an unusually vocal stand against graft within the country's multi-layered bureaucracy, and the party vowed to root out corruption in a policy document issued at its congress.
However, Manh said the National Assembly would not be able to pass an anti-corruption law during its current session.
Communist Party Secretary General Do Muoi told local reporters earlier in the week that he favoured such a law and the creation of a special committee to lead the battle against graft.
